text: Now flip it around. What if the person on the other side reads the rules better than the company?

In 1999, Healthy Choice offered airline miles for barcodes from its products: five hundred miles for ten barcodes, doubled if you mailed them early. Engineer David Phillips looked for the cheapest barcode in the store. Chocolate pudding. Twenty-five cents a cup.

He bought over twelve thousand cups, had Salvation Army volunteers peel the barcodes, and gave the pudding to people in need. About three thousand dollars turned into over a million miles. The donation even got him a tax write-off, and Hollywood later borrowed his pudding plan for an Adam Sandler movie.

He didn't cheat. He did exactly what the rules paid for. The company wanted people to buy its food. It paid for barcodes. And a barcode is just a barcode. Phillips later put it simply: "Companies still make mistakes like this all the time."
